newsitem.title: USA: Midwest utilities unfairly blamed - AEP.
newsitem.headline: Midwest utilities unfairly blamed - AEP.

text.p: Electric utilities in the Midwest are being unfairly blamed as a significant cause of air quality problems in the Northeast, according to American Electric Power Co Inc chief executive E. Linn Draper Jr.

"The most recent Ozone Transport Assessment Group modeling, released just last month, was said to show that Midwest emissions controls -- in Ohio, for example -- could help the Northeast ozone situation," Draper told The Energy Daily "Environmental Effects of Retail Wheeling" conference Thursday. "How much? Two to six parts per billion.

"On a bad day in New York City, that would come off their level of 140 or 160 parts per billion," Draper said, noting that Midwest emissions controls would not bring the Northeast close to the current standard of 120 parts per million.
Stating "cost of the Midwest controls would be in the billions of dollars," he added "The math is not complicated. The solution would not be effective and it would not be cost-effective."
Draper said the issue is not whether or not emissions can cross state boundaries. The issue is distance.

"The indicators are clear so far that long-distance ozone transport from the Midwest to the Northeast is not significant, and reduced emissions from Midwest power plants would do extremely little to benefit the Northeast," he said.
Draper also cautioned against attempts to link environmental issues with efforts to bring competition to the electric industry.

"We must keep in mind that environmental concerns are not the same as some other issues linked to the onset of electricity competition, such as stranded commitments or grid reliability, for example," he said, noting efforts to complicate electric industry deregulation with environmental issues may be driven by other reasons.
"As restructuring of the electric industry proceeds, there are various stakeholders who see in that process the opportunity to advance their particular agendas," Draper said.

"Clearly, environmental impact is an agenda item that can be tugged and pulled in varying directions. Some of those waving the banner of environmental protection would appear to see it as a means to hold back the electricity competition they are not ready for."
